defense_analyst.prose: Washington's defense leans on extra rushers. It sends five or more on 42.6% of dropbacks [dc1] over 333 plays [dc2], the third-highest blitz rate in the league [dc3], and averages 4.6 rushers per dropback [dc4]. That produces a pressure proxy of 14.1% [dc5] and a sack rate of 5.1% [dc6]. The cost shows in pass EPA, which is 0.07 per play allowed [dc7], so the blitz is a gamble that can leave the back end exposed. NYG's offense sits at 0.00 EPA per play [dc8] over 515 plays [dc9], and it has allowed a pressure proxy of 18.6% [dc10] on 301 dropbacks [dc11]. That is the matchup to attack: if NYG's protection breaks down, the extra rushers will get home, so the staff should check quick game and hot throws against the blitz. Washington's run defense is stout, allowing -0.06 EPA per run play [dc12] on 183 runs [dc13], with explosive runs at 5.5% [dc14] and 6.7 defenders in the box on average [dc15]. NYG should expect light boxes to be punished less often than heavy ones, but the run game is the way to keep the pass rush off the field. Explosive pass plays allowed sit at 7.5% [dc16]. Third down is a clear weakness: Washington lets 40.4% convert [dc17] on 109 attempts [dc18], and it has allowed touchdowns on 75.0% of red-zone drives [dc19], though that rests on only 28 drives [dc20], so the sample is small.
